title: Probability: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
lead: Because every particle is a wave, no one can predict where a single electron will land, only the pattern that many of them build. Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle limits how precisely position and momentum, and energy and time, can be known together.
objectives: Use both versions of Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle in calculations.
Explain the implications of Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle for measurements.
summary_html:
• Matter is found to have the same interference characteristics as any other wave.
  • There is now a probability distribution for the location of a particle rather than a definite position.
  • Another consequence of the wave character of all particles is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which limits the precision with which certain physical quantities can be known simultaneously. For position and momentum, the uncertainty principle is $\kdx\,\kdp \ge \frac{h}{4\pi}$, where $\kdx$ is the uncertainty in position and $\kdp$ is the uncertainty in momentum.
  • For energy and time, the uncertainty principle is $\kdE\,\kdt \ge \frac{h}{4\pi}$ where $\kdE$ is the uncertainty in energy and $\kdt$ is the uncertainty in time.
  • These small limits are fundamentally important on the quantum-mechanical scale.
notes: Five of the module’s ten problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the chlorine ion located to 1.00 μm, the proton whose velocity is known to 0.250% of the speed of light, the nucleus with a lifetime of 10⁻²⁰ s, the nuclear excited state with a 2.0-eV uncertainty, and the derivation of ΔEΔt ≈ h. The text says the double-slit equation was developed in Photon Energies and the Electromagnetic Spectrum, where it was in fact developed in Wave Optics, and this is kept as printed.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 29.21) The building up of the diffraction pattern of electrons scattered from a crystal surface. Each electron arrives at a definite location, which cannot be precisely predicted. The overall distribution shown at the bottom can be predicted as the diffraction of waves having the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons. (Figure 29.22) Double-slit interference for electrons (a) and photons (b) is identical for equal wavelengths and equal slit separations. Both patterns are probability distributions in the sense that they are built up by individual particles traversing the apparatus, the paths of which are not individually predictable.

exercises.prompt: What is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle? Does it place limits on what can be known?

answer.solution: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle says that you cannot measure certain pairs of quantities both to exact precision at the same time. For position and momentum, $\kdx\,\kdp \ge h/4\pi$, and for energy and time, $\kdE\,\kdt \ge h/4\pi$. It does limit what anyone can know, even in principle. To locate a particle you must probe it with something of short wavelength, and that probe carries a large momentum that changes the particle’s momentum by an unknowable amount. Neither uncertainty can be zero, and making one smaller makes the other larger. Because $h$ is so small, the limit matters only on the scale of atoms and smaller; for large objects it is negligible.

exercises.prompt: (a) If the position of an electron in a membrane is measured to an accuracy of $1.00\;\mu\text{m}$, what is the electron’s minimum uncertainty in velocity? (b) If the electron has this velocity, what is its kinetic energy in eV? (c) What are the implications of this energy, comparing it to typical molecular binding energies?

parts.hint: Use $\frac{1}{2}m\kv^{2}$ with the speed from (a), and divide by $1.60\times 10^{-19}$ J/eV.

answer.solution: (a) 57.9 m/s (b) $9.55\times 10^{-9}\;\text{eV}$ (c) From Table 29.1, typical molecular binding energies range from about 1 eV to 10 eV, therefore the result in part (b) is approximately 9 orders of magnitude smaller than typical molecular binding energies.

exercises.prompt: Suppose the velocity of an electron in an atom is known to an accuracy of $2.0\times 10^{3}\;\text{m/s}$ (reasonably accurate compared with orbital velocities). What is the electron’s minimum uncertainty in position, and how does this compare with the approximate 0.1-nm size of the atom?

parts.part: how many times the size of the atom
parts.hint: Divide the uncertainty in position by 0.1 nm.

exercises.prompt: A relatively long-lived excited state of an atom has a lifetime of 3.00 ms. What is the minimum uncertainty in its energy?

answer.hint: Use $\kdE = h/4\pi\kdt$ with $\kdt = 3.00\times 10^{-3}$ s, and convert to eV.

exercises.prompt: The decay energy of a short-lived particle has an uncertainty of 1.0 MeV due to its short lifetime. What is the smallest lifetime it can have?

answer.hint: Use $\kdt = h/4\pi\kdE$ with $\kdE = 1.0\times 10^{6}$ eV written in joules.

exercises.prompt: What is the approximate uncertainty in the mass of a muon, as determined from its decay lifetime?

answer.hint: The muon lives about $2.2\times 10^{-6}$ s. Find $\kdE = h/4\pi\kdt$, then the uncertainty in mass is $\kdE/c^{2}$.
